summary: A 1975 list of references and contacts about the various protocols used on the ARPANET, along with recent developments. It updates RFC 661.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the up-to-date directory of which documents and people to check for each network rule.

subtitle: Jon Postel's June 1975 directory of ARPANET protocols, their documents, contacts and latest news.

tldr.problem: ARPANET protocol work was scattered across many RFCs, reports and people, and newcomers had no single place to see what existed.
tldr.mechanism: This file lists each protocol with its contact, documents, people, schedule, comments and recent developments, marking official standards with [Official].
tldr.outcome: It was meant to be kept current with help from users of the file, and it points to online copies and to liaison lists for finding people.

facts.label: Messages in transit per host pair

today: RFC 694 updates RFC 661. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no RFC obsoleting it, but it is a June 1975 snapshot of a living list, so its schedules and news are long out of date.

sections.title: How the File Works
sections.content:
RFC 694 is a compendium of protocol activity on the ARPA Network, maintained by Jon Postel at SRI-ARC with help from readers who send news and corrections. Most activity is with experimental protocols; those that are official standards have "[Official]" after the name.

It points to online copies of recent RFCs and to related files: the official host names (RFC 608), and two lists of Network Liaisons, the contacts designated by host organizations. The Network Information Center (NIC) provides file space and keeps a hardcopy library of all RFCs, and filed the collection "ARPA Network Current Network Protocols" (as of 1-December-74) with the National Technical Information Service.
sections.plainLanguage: It explains how the directory is kept up to date and where to find other lists like names and contact people.

sections.title: Network-Level Protocols
sections.content:
The first entries cover the lower levels. For IMP-IMP and IMP-HOST (official), the text notes that the "link number" field was extended from 8 to 12 bits and renamed the message identification field, and that up to eight messages may be in transit between a source and destination host. BBN Report 1822 was updated to include the Pluribus IMP and the uncontrolled packet. Proposed changes are discussed in RFC 687 and RFC 690.

HOST-HOST entries cover the official NCP, an experimental variant with reliability improvements (RFC 636), and a lost-message proposal (RFC 663). Other entries include the Message Switching Protocol, the Network Voice Protocol, packet radio, host-front end, and the PARC Universal Protocol (link 151 assigned).

The TCP entry reports experiments and implementations: the BBN version at BBN-TENEXA, an SU-DSL version for the PDP-11/20 in debugging, and a UCL (London) PDP-9 version in coding. It says an international form of TCP with a 144-bit header instead of 256 bits and no three-way handshake was the most likely international standard.
sections.plainLanguage: These entries cover how machines and the network boxes talk, plus early experiments like voice and radio, and an early version of the protocol that became TCP.

sections.title: Telnet, FTP and Mail
sections.content:
Telnet has Old and New versions; the New Telnet [Official] has options numbered 0 to 16 plus 255 (Extended Options List), including Transmit Binary, Echo, Suppress Go Ahead, Status and Timing Mark. Hosts were to run it by 1 January 1974, with the server on socket 23 decimal (27 octal). Recent items are the survey in RFC 679 and the TIP schedule in RFC 688.

FTP entries list Old and New file transfer. Recent news includes TENEX paged-file extensions (RFC 683) and Brian Harvey's suggestion in RFC 691 to fix old FTP instead of moving to a new one. Mail entries cover the current mail based on RFC 454, RFC 680 header formats and RFC 630 error code usage, plus proposed mail protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The remote login, file sending and mail sections each list the current rules, the newer proposals and the people to ask.

sections.title: Services, Programs and the National Software Works
sections.content:
Later entries cover remote job entry (RJE and CCN's RJS), graphics, the Data Reconfiguration Service, RSEXEC, and the Line Processor protocol, then programs such as the network standard editor NETED and the Unified User-Level Protocol (also known as the Common Command Language).

The final part describes the National Software Works (NSW) and its Distributed Programming System, which shares resources at the subroutine level and splits NLS into front-end and back-end parts. It lists documents such as the Procedure Call Protocol (PCP), the Procedure Interface Package, the Process Management Package and the File Package. These documents describe the state of January 1975 and are generally descriptive rather than definitive.
sections.plainLanguage: The end of the file covers higher-level tools and one big project to share programs across machines, with a reading list for each.
